3. Briefly stated the plaintiffs case is that Hemanta Kumar Ghosh and others, the land-lords purchased in auction their aiyati interest of one Golam Ali Sk. on 4.9.34 which was sold in execution of rent decree vide rent execution case No. 1918 of 1934 and took delivery of possession on 31.1.55. This raiyati interests comprised 4.48 acres of land in a kbatian no 188. Within this raiyati interest k was an under tenancy comprising. 10 decimals of land which was annulled by the Ghosh landlords by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. The plaintiff thereafter took settlement of the entire laud measuring 3.48 acres from the Ghosh landlords by executing a regd. kabuliyat dated 25th Baishak, 1342 .B.S. corresponding to 8.5.35 at a rental of Rs. 6-5 anas. Since then he has been in possession of the land on payment of rent for which he got dakhilas from the Government, The defendants constructed 3 huts of golpata in Asar, 1367 B.S. on 10 decimals of land .and got this piece of land recorded in the record of rights prepared after State acquisition. Hence the suit. 

 4. Defendant nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement to the effect that there was no auction purchase or delivery of possession and no notice was served under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, their interest was never annulled and they have been continuously in possession of the suit land althrough. 

 5. The main point for consideration before the courts below was whether the plain-tiff had any right, title, interest and possession.: in the suit land comprising 10 decimals of south east portion of plot NO. 66 of kbatian No. 188/1. This point is dependant on whether the Ghosh landlords after purchasing the raiyati interest of Golam Ali SK. in execution of the rent decree, annulled the incumbrance of the defendants by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, and thereafter settled the entire raiyati interests with the plaintiff free from all encumbrances as recited in the registered Kabuliyat dated .8-5-35 executed by the plaintiff. 6. The learned Munsif after discussing the evidence on record held: defendants cannot say that their under tenancy was never annulled. On the other band the Additional Subordinate Judge on the basis of the same evidence found; “Thus upon the evidence, the story of khas possession either by the Ghash landlords or their lessee, the plaintiff has not 'been proved and that shows that the korfa of the defendants does not-stand disturbed and shall be deemed to have been continuing as before." 

 7. Mr. Sk. Razzaque Ali, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plain-tiff-appellant has urged that on the face of preponderance of evidence on record which he has referred to, in the course of his sub-mission, the lower appellate court erred in law in not holding that the tenancy of the defendants was not annulled. 

 9. The learned Counsel for the contesting respondents has further relied upon two decisions, one of the Calcutta High Court Tayefa Khatun Choudhurani vs. Sornadhan  K. Sen Rai reported in 53(1931) Calcutta Law journal page 512 and another of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, Nirode Baran Va. Devendra Mohan reported in BCR 309 (AD) in support , of his contention that , the provision of section 167 of the Bengal, Tenancy Act has not been complied with in the instant case. The facts and circumstances of these cases referred to above are quite different from those of the instant case. The Calcutta case lays down that sec.167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act is intended to ,Offer a choice to the purchaser of a tenure under a rent decree either to accept the under tenure or to avoid it within a year. If the purchaser does not exercise the right to annul the encumbrance within the time allowed, by law, it must be presumed that he intends to adopt the under tenure or any other encumbrance created by the last tenant. This is a correct interpretation of the section. But in the instant case the main point for consideration is not the requirement of that section but whether or not the annulment of the encumbrance by the Ghosh landlords in accordance with the provisions of section 167 of that Act has been proved by the evidence on record. 

 10.  In the appellate Division case the question of annulment was under consideration. and both the courts below as well as the High Court Division in second appeal found on discussion of evidence that the under tenancy was not extinguished by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. That being a question of fact and decided by all the court's below the Appellate Division held that no interference was called for. 

 11. It is the case of the plaintiff that Golam Ali Sk. held the raiyati interest under the Glaosh landlord in Khatian No. 188 and under Golam Ali Kohiluddin, defendant No. 1, his brother Fatik father of defendants Nos. 2, 3 and 4 and Yousuf held an under tenancy in Khatian No.188(1). Admittedly the plaintiff could not file any paper to show directly the annulment of this under tenancy in accordance with section 167 of the Bangal Tenancy Act. The learned Advocate for the 5 appellant submits that mere non-production of the notice under section 167 or paper connected with the service of such notice by itself Would not be fatal for the plaintiff's case if it could be proved otherwise that there was service of such notice and the encumbrance was, in fact, annulled. 

 12. The under-tenancy was held by defendant No. 1 Kohiluddin Sk. his brother Fatik Sk., the father of defendant No. 2, 3 and 4 and one Yousuf Sk. It is on evidence that the interest of Yousuf Sk. was purchased by the plaintiff long before the aforesaid rent execution case. Ext. 4 is the registered kabuliyat dated 8.5.35 executed by plaintiff in favour of the ex-landlords. It has been mentioned in the recital of the kabuliyat that the plaintiff is taking settlement of the entire land measuring 3.48 acres from the said Ghosh landlords free from all incumbrance. It is interesting to note that Fatik, father of defendant No.2 to 4 was attesting witness of this kabuliyat and also identified Abdul Sk., the executant, i.e. the plaintiff herein and it is also interesting to note that only one of Fatik's sons and Fatik's brother Kohiluddin Sk. are the only contesting parties. It is true that a document is not binding on a person who is not a party to it but such a document is admissible in evidence under section 13 of the Evidence Act as an instance of assertion of right even though it is not inter parties and weight is given to the recital in an old document though not inter parties particularly when the recital in the document is acted upon. 

 13. It is further seen from the evidence that Yousuf, one of the co-sharers of Fatiq and of defendant No. 1 Kohiluddin, attested the writ of delivery of possession dated 31.1.35 (Ext. 6) made in pursuance of the auction sale referred to above. Furthermore, the plaintiff has produced dahlias (Ext. 1 series) to show that he paid rent in respect of the entire tenancy which he took settlement from the Ghosh landlord. He paid rent to the ex-landlords and after state acquisition of rent-receiving interests to the Government. 

 15. As against the dakhilas submitted by the plaintiff in support of his case and also indicating the facts of his exercise of rights of ownership of the entire land measuring 3.48 acres taken by him by way of settlement from the Ghosh landlords, the defendants could not produce any dakhila or paper to show that they ever paid any rent to anybody in respect of the under-tenancy they claim to have been holding from a long period of time. It indicates that they have been acting upon the premise of annulment of their under tenancy. 16. It is further found from the evidence on record that the plaintiff (as P.W. 1) deposed that the under-tenancy in question was annulled by serving notice under section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, the notice was served on the land by hanging a copy there of on a bamboo slip in the disputed land and possession thereof was taken by beat of drum in the summer season and he was present at that time He further said that defendant No.1 Kohiluddin constructed hut on the disputed land in Asar, 1367 B.S. in spite of his opposition and this  was known to Opazuddin, P.W. 5 who corroborates  the plaintiff on this point. P.W. 2 Kayemuddin Sk, also spoke of the construction of huts by the defendants in. 1367 B.S. P.W. 3, Mohiuddin a former Tahsildar of the Ghosh lands proved the dakhilas issued by them. 

 19. In the instant case the deposition of P.Ws. 1; 2, 3 and 5 Coupled with the documentary evidence Exta. 1 series; 3, 4, 5 and 6 unmistakably lead to the irresistible conclusion that the under-raiyati interests of the defendants stood annulled and the defendants themselves also acted upon the promise of annulment of their interest by refraining from paying any rent in respect of that interest thereafter to anybody. In the face of all these weighty evidences it cannot be held as has been erroneously done by the lower appellate court that the under-tenancy of the defendants was not annulled.
